## Abstract

A weighted directed graph G is a triple (V, A, g) where (V, A) is a directed graph and g is an arbitrary real-valued function defined on the arc set A. Let G be a strongly-connected, simple weighted directed graph. We say that G is max-balanced if for every nontrivial subset of the vertices W, the maximum weight over arcs leaving W equals the maximum weight over arcs entering W. We show that there exists a (up to an additive constant) unique potential p_{v} for v ∈ V such that (V, A, g^{p}) is max-balanced where g_{a}^{p} = p_{u} + g_{a} − p_{v} for a = (u, v) ∈ A. We describe an O(|V|^{2}|A|) algorithm for computing p using an algorithm for computing the maximum cycle-mean of G. Finally, we apply our principal result to the similarity scaling of nonnegative matrices.

## Abstract

We study a special three-sided matching game, the so-called supplier-firm-buyer game, in which buyers and sellers (suppliers) trade indirectly through middlemen (firms). Stuart (1997) showed that all supplier-firm-buyer games have non-empty core. We show that for these games the core coincides with the classical bargaining set (Davis and Maschler, 1967), and also with the Mas-Colell bargaining set (Mas-Colell, 1989).

## Introduction

In their seminal paper Shapley and Shubik (1972) introduced assignment games to study two-sided matching markets where there are indivisible goods which are traded between sellers and buyers in exchange for money. Their proof of the non-emptiness of the core established a fruitful research area. Multi-sided assignment games, however, have different features. Most importantly, the non-emptiness of the core is not guaranteed anymore even when there are only three sides in the game, as first demonstrated by Kaneko and Wooders (1982).

Since the core may be empty for multi-sided assignment games, some authors study conditions to obtain the non-emptiness of the core (see for instance Quint (1991), Stuart (1997), Sherstyuk (1999), Atay and Núñez (2017)). In this paper, we focus on the class introduced by Brandenburger and Stuart (1996) and investigated by Stuart (1997). In the so-called supplier-firm-buyer games, agents in the market are partitioned into three sides and the groups are arranged along a chain. Sellers (suppliers) and buyers (customers) are at the two ends of the chain, but trade between them can only be made via agents in the middle (firms). The valuation on the supplier-firm-buyer triplets is locally additive, it sums up the potential values of the supplier-firm and of the firm-buyer matchings, but it is realized only if all three parties cooperate. Stuart (1997) showed that all supplier-firm-buyer games have non-empty core.

In order to find plausible payoff allocations even in games with empty core, Aumann and Maschler (1964) suggested a set-valued solution concept that incorporates some negotiating possibilities of the players. Among the various bargaining sets proposed, the one investigated by Davis and Maschler (1967) has emerged, for it was proved to be non-empty whenever the game has a non-empty imputation set (Davis and Maschler, 1967). Mas-Colell (1989) introduced another bargaining set notion based on preimputations and showed that it is non-empty for any game. (Holzman, 2001) proved that for superadditive games the classical (Davis–Maschler) bargaining set is included in the Mas-Colell bargaining set.

# Strict chain markets: a proved dimension-independent protection theorem

5 September 2026. One bounded theory follow-up. This is a mathematical derivation, not a priority finding. The representation and the general directed-cycle argument may have classical predecessors; external novelty remains unassessed. No manuscript was changed.

## Statement

There are m players in each of three sectors. Only triples produce value, with

w_ijk = P_ij + Q_jk,   P,Q >= 0.

Let K be the entire core, T>0 the integral matching value, x the full ascending-sorted leximin payoff, and H_a=max_{y in K} y_a. Then

x_a >= H_a/3 for every player a,
||x-y||_1/T <= 4/3 for every y in K.

In particular the distance bound applies to the full descending-sorted lexicographic minimum. Both constants are sharp across this class: complete player-additive arrays are a subclass and supply the already established 1/3 ideal-share example and distance supremum 4/3. The distance supremum need not be attained by one finite market.

No smaller coalition receives direct bilateral worth in this statement. Every player remains in the payoff vector, including fixed-zero coordinates. The core is a nonempty compact convex polytope: all payoffs are nonnegative with fixed finite total T, and only finitely many linear constraints occur. Full leximin therefore exists and has a unique labeled payoff vector, as can be obtained by successively fixing every coordinate forced at each optimal floor. The potential representation below is injective because the outer-sector player payoffs recover all nonanchor potentials.

## 1. Exact core representation

Choose optimal perfect matchings in P and Q. They can be joined through their middle-sector agents into a triple matching. Each triple matching projects to bilateral matchings, so this joined matching has optimal total T equal to the sum of the two bilateral optimal values. Relabel the first and third sectors to make both chosen bilateral matchings diagonal. Set s_j=P_jj+Q_jj.

Write payoffs (u,v,z) in sector order. Matching efficiency forces u_j+v_j+z_j=s_j. The entire core is exactly

u_j>=0, z_j>=0, v_j=s_j-u_j-z_j>=0,
u_i-u_j >= P_ij-P_jj for all i,j,
z_k-z_j >= Q_jk-Q_jj for all j,k.

Necessity of the last two inequalities follows from triples (i,j,j) and (j,j,k). Conversely their sum is the inequality for arbitrary triple (i,j,k). This proves equality with the full core, not merely inclusion of a convenient face. Nonemptiness also follows by adding nonnegative optimal bilateral dual payoffs at each middle player; nonnegative matrices admit such bilateral optimal duals.

## 2. A general directed-cycle certificate lemma

Consider a finite directed graph with node potentials q, one anchor potential fixed at zero. Every arc e=(tail,head) has a nonnegative slack

s_e(q)=c_e+q_tail-q_head >=0.

Some arcs are designated as player payoffs; the remaining arcs impose structural constraints. Suppose the feasible payoff set has a full leximin vector x. Fix a player arc e and let alpha=x_e. Form D from:

- every structural arc that is tight at x;
- every player arc f whose payoff x_f<=alpha.

Then D contains a directed path from head(e) to tail(e).

Proof. If there is no such path, let S be the nodes that can reach tail(e) in D, including tail(e) itself. The head of e is not in S. Set h=1 on S and h=0 outside S. Every arc a->b of D satisfies h_a>=h_b: otherwise a reaches a node that reaches tail(e), contrary to a outside S. Subtract the anchor's h value from all h values to keep the anchor fixed; potential differences do not change.

Moving q a sufficiently small positive amount in direction h increases player e, decreases no player with payoff <=alpha, and harms no tight structural constraint. All other structural constraints have positive slack, and all other player payoffs exceed alpha, so finiteness permits a common positive step that preserves feasibility and leaves any decreasing payoff above alpha. The sorted payoff vector strictly improves lexicographically. This contradicts full leximin. Therefore the path exists.

This cut argument does not require the graph to be connected: all nodes outside the backward-reachable set receive the same initial zero perturbation, and the common anchor shift preserves every difference. Choose a simple such path. Together with e it forms a simple directed cycle Z. Its structural arcs are tight at x, and all its player arcs have payoffs <=x_e. Potential differences telescope around Z. Consequently, for every feasible y,

sum_{player arcs f in Z} y_f <= sum_{f in Z} c_f
                              = sum_{player arcs f in Z} x_f.

The first inequality uses nonnegativity of the structural slacks at y; the equality uses their tightness at x. In particular, if Z contains at most r player arcs then

y_e <= r*x_e.

Zero payoffs require no separate exception: the same argument shows that a leximin-zero player belonging to such a certificate is fixed at zero throughout the feasible set.

## 3. Apply the certificate to strict chains

Introduce nodes 0, U_j, Z_j and potentials

q_0=0, q_{U_j}=u_j, q_{Z_j}=-z_j.

The three types of player arcs and their slacks are

U_j -> 0:       u_j,
0 -> Z_j:       z_j,
Z_j -> U_j:     s_j-u_j-z_j = v_j.

All structural arcs stay within one layer:

U_i -> U_j, constant P_jj-P_ij,
Z_j -> Z_k, constant Q_jj-Q_jk.

Their slacks are precisely the two difference-constraint systems in Section 1.

Every simple directed cycle containing a player arc has exactly three player arcs, one from each sector. Indeed, the only transition from the Z layer to the U layer is a middle-player arc; the only way back passes through 0, using one first-sector and one third-sector arc. A simple cycle visits 0 at most once. Structural arcs cannot change layers. This also covers a cycle initially specified through an outer-sector player arc.

The certificate lemma with r=3 now gives y_a<=3*x_a for every player and every y in K. Maximizing over y proves H_a<=3*x_a.

Finally, min(x_a,y_a)>=y_a/3. Both payoff vectors are nonnegative with total T, so

||x-y||_1 = 2*(T-sum_a min(x_a,y_a)) <= 4*T/3.

This establishes the statement for the entire core and full leximin, without deleting dummy players or replacing leximin by an arbitrary first-stage maximin optimizer.

## 4. Sharpness and research consequence

The complete player-additive family w_ijk=1+1_{i=1}+1_{j=1} lies in the chain class by taking P_ij=1+1_{i=1}+1_{j=1} and Q_jk=0. With m>=2 its entire-core calculations already in the consolidated paper give the sharp ideal fraction 1/3 and full-selector distance 4m/[3(m+2)], which tends to 4/3.

Together with the independently checked triangle-of-pair-gains example having fraction 5/18, the theorem distinguishes chain interaction from cyclic pair interaction at the 1/3 guarantee. It does not establish that cyclic interaction destroys every positive dimension-independent guarantee. It also does not show that cyclic pair-additive distance exceeds 4/3.

A concrete useful artifact is the per-player certificate: a directed cycle with one player per sector, all three leximin payoffs at most the target's, whose structural arcs are tight. This certificate certifies the target's ideal bound by an ordinary sum of inequalities. Priority review should compare this argument with classical max-min fairness for potential/slack networks and locally additive assignment markets before calling it new.

Research Institute for Discrete Mathematics, University of Bonn

ABSTRACT
In this paper we present a new method for clock scheduling
and clocktree construction that improves the performance of
high-end ASICs signiﬁcantly.
First, we compute a clock schedule that yields the optimum
cycle time and the best possible clock distribution with respect
to early and late mode; in particular the number of critical
tests is minimized. Second, individual arrival time intervals
are computed for all endpoints of the clocktree. Finally, we
construct a clocktree that realizes arrival times within these
intervals and exploits positive slacks to save power consump-
tion.
We demonstrate the superiority of our method to previous
approaches by experimental results on industrial ASICs with
up to 194 000 registers and more than 160 clock domains. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Games on Debruijn Graphs and Cycle Means

10 Pages Posted: 10 Jan 2025

## Nadejda Drenska

Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge

### Abstract

deBruijn graphs are widely used in genomics and computer science. In this paper we present a novel approach to finding weights on edges of doubly weighted deBruijn graphs. Given any fixed set of weights on vertices, we use a repeated two-person zero-sum game to find weights on edges so that every cycle on the deBruijn graph has the same average weight, providing explicit formulas. This approach uses minimax optimal strategies of the players. Once the weights on the edges are determined, we observe that they correspond to solving a set of linear equations with as many equations as there are cycles. This is very surprising, because there are many more cycles than unknowns. Moreover we analyze other, related games on graphs.

Keywords: deBruijn graph, repeated two-person game, cycle mean

The mean weight of a cycle in an edge-weighted graph is the sum of the cycle's edge weights divided by the cycle's length. We study the minimum mean-weight cycle on the complete graph on n vertices, with random i.i.d. edge weights drawn from an exponential distribution with mean 1. We show that the probability of the min mean weight being at most c/n tends to a limiting function of c which is analytic for c ≤ 1/e, discontinuous at c = 1/e, and equal to 1 for c > 1/e. L7@P0: ABSTRACT
L8@P0: In this paper we present a new method for clock scheduling
L9@P0: and clocktree construction that improves the performance of
L10@P0: high-end ASICs significantly.
L11@P0: First, we compute a clock schedule that yields the optimum
L12@P0: cycle time and the best possible clock distribution with respect
L13@P0: to early and late mode; in particular the number of critical
L14@P0: tests is minimized. Second, individual arrival time intervals
L15@P0: are computed for all endpoints of the clocktree. Finally, we
L16@P0: construct a clocktree that realizes arrival times within these
L17@P0: intervals and exploits positive slacks to save power consumption.
L18@P0: We demonstrate the superiority of our method to previous
L19@P0: approaches by experimental results on industrial ASICs with
L20@P0: up to 194 000 registers and more than 160 clock domains. We
L21@P0: improved the clock frequencies by 5-28% up to 1.033 GHz (in
L22@P0: hardware).
L23@P0: 1. INTRODUCTION
L24@P0: Due to increase of clock frequencies and design sizes clocktree
L25@P0: construction has become one of the most challenging problems in
L26@P0: VLSI-design. There is an extensive literature. Most works either
L27@P0: focus on clock scheduling or on clocktree construction without optimizing schedules.
L28@P0: A linear programming formulation for cycle time optimization
L29@P0: by clock scheduling can be found [9, 16]. Shortest path approaches
L30@P0: from graph theory were proposed in [6, 17, 18]. Scheduling techniques that optimize not only the cycle time but also less critical
L31@P0: cycles were developed in [1, 14].
L32@P0: Most papers on clocktree construction aim at zero-skew trees
L33@P0: or bounded-skew trees and are based on the deferred-mergeembedding algorithm [3, 5, 8, 20]. Methods for integrated
L34@P0: buffer/inverter insertion are given in [4, chapter 5], which also
L35@P0: gives an overview on the topic.
L36@P0: Kourtev and Friedman proposed a simultaneous clock scheduling and clocktree synthesis [12]. In [13] they considered a
L37@P0: quadratic programming approach to increase reliability of the
L38@P0: clock schedule. An overview on their work can be found in [14].
L39@P0: Individual skew bounds for each register pair are considered in
L40@P0: [15, 19, 22].
L41@P0: All previous works concerning clock scheduling used a register
L42@P0: graph, consisting of all registers as nodes and having arcs representing the minimum and maximum delay of data paths between
L43@P0: these registers. However, the size of the register graph, with a
L44@P0: potentially quadratic number of arcs, proves impracticable for designs with several hundred thousand registers.
L45@P0: Instead, we apply clock scheduling based on a slack balance
L46@P0: graph that is based on the timing graph. The size of the slack
L47@P0: balance graph is proportional to the size of the netlist, which is
L48@P0: typically linear in the number of registers. In particular we can
L49@P0: handle very complex chips with many clock domains and complicated timing assertions.
L50@P0: We then apply the minimum balance algorithm [1, 23]. Our
L51@P0: clock schedule computation optimizes slacks below a threshold
L52@P0: and additionally distributes remaining positive slacks to required
L53@P0: clock arrival time intervals. These intervals are used to construct
L54@P0: low-power clocktrees.
L55@P0: Clocktree construction is done by a bottom-up algorithm. We
L56@P0: obtain the necessary skews by varying the number of stages and
L57@P0: the inverter types but not by routing detours. The placement of the
L58@P0: inverters (avoiding blockages) and the choice of the inverter sizes
L59@P0: is done late in the algorithm to save power consumption.
L60@P0: Our experimental results prove that this approach is feasible
L61@P0: even for the most complex ASICs that are designed today. We improve clock frequencies and power consumption simultaneously.

L142@P1: Our main goal is to maximize the worst slack. The next goal is to
L143@P1: maximize the second smallest slack, and so on. More precisely, we

L145@P1: nondecreasing order, is lexicographically maximum. This problem
L146@P1: can be solved by applying the minimum balance algorithm [1, 23]

L151@P1: V (G). Additionally V (G) contains an extra node v˜ that represents the time origin (zero time). Every arrival time can now be
L152@P1: represented by a node potential. We introduce an arc from node

L210@P2: As we build up the slack balance graph, arcs representing test

L217@P2: test arcs at once. Early mode problems (violations of (2), (4), (6)

L267@P2-3: 2344. CLOCKTREE DESIGN
L268@P3: Up to now we have shown how to compute optimal arrival time
L269@P3: intervals for the clocktree endpoints. In this section we will present
L270@P3: a method to build a clocktree that can realize these intervals.
L271@P3: In addition to the sinks provided with arrival time interval, position in the plane and required parity, we are given a source with
L272@P3: its position, starttime, startparity and startslew. As repower circuits we allow a set of inverters inverterset with timing rules and
L273@P3: bounds on the capacitance they can drive. Moreover, we have a set
L274@P3: of rectangular blockages blockageset, a slew bound maxslew,
L275@P3: and a maximum distance between two adjacent vertices (pins in
L276@P3: the same net) maxdist, in order to bound wire delay.
L277@P3: The task is now to build an arborescence G = (V, E), where
L278@P3: the leaves are the sinks, the root is the source, and the internal vertices are inverters in inverterset. Moreover, the internal vertices
L279@P3: have to be placed whithin the chip area outside the blockages, and
L280@P3: the capacitance limits of the inverters, the slew limit (maxslew)
L281@P3: and the distance limit (maxdist) must be kept. We have to ensure
L282@P3: that a signal starting at the source with the given starttime, startslew and startparity reaches each sink within its time interval and
L283@P3: with the required parity. The secondary goal is to minimize power
L284@P3: consumption.
L285@P3: We will generate the clocktree in a bottom-up manner. The vertices will not be placed until they have got a predecessor. For
L286@P3: each vertex we determine an area where we can place it, and an
L287@P3: area where we can possibly place its predecessor. All areas which
L288@P3: appear in the algorithm will be finite unions of octagons, whose
L289@P3: angles are multiples of 45◦. By storing an octagon as the intersection of two rectangles, one axis-parallel and one rotated by 45◦
L290@P3: , all
L291@P3: necessary operations (e.g. intersection of two areas, etc.) can be
L292@P3: performed efficiently.
L293@P3: The assignment of the internal vertices to the inverters is fixed at
L294@P3: the very end, after the whole tree has been built. While constructing the vertices we will compute a set of ’solution candidates’ for
L295@P3: each newly generated vertex. Each solution candidate consists of
L296@P3: an inverter for the vertex and a pointer to a solution candidate of
L297@P3: each successor. Using these candidates, a time interval for each
L298@P3: internal vertex is computed. The time intervals of the sinks are the
L299@P3: given required arrival time intervals.
L300@P3: We call a vertex active as long as it does not have a predecessor.
L301@P3: 4.1. Main Algorithm
L302@P3: At the beginning, the clocktree just consists of the sinks as leaves
L303@P3: of the tree with their corresponding time intervals and required
L304@P3: parities. They are all active. The active vertices will be stored in
L305@P3: two sets, according to their expected parity.
L306@P3: In each iteration of the main loop a new vertex is generated. The
L307@P3: successors of the new vertex are computed using a greedy clustering strategy. The first successor is an active vertex with maximum
L308@P3: lower bound of its arrival time interval. In section 4.2 the choice
L309@P3: of the other successors will be described.
L310@P3: In the next step the position of the successors, which have become inactive now, are fixed. Then we compute the areas where
L311@P3: the new vertex and its predecessor can be placed (section 4.3).
L312@P3: Finally we have to specify a set of solution candidates for the
L313@P3: new vertex (section 4.4).
L314@P3: The algorithm terminates the main loop when all remaining active vertices can be connected to the source. Now the topology of
L315@P3: the clocktree and its embedding are determined. In the last iteration a set of solution candidates for the source is computed. We
L316@P3: choose the solution candidate that has minimum power consumption among those yielding the best realization of the starttime and
L317@P3: assign the inverters according to this solution.
L318@P3: 4.2. Clustering
L319@P3: The clustering determines the successors of a new vertex.
L320@P3: A cluster of successors for a new vertex is feasible if the following conditions hold:
L321@P3: 1. the new vertex can be placed so that its distance to each successor is at most maxdist,
L322@P3: 2. the intersection of the time intervals of all successors is not
L323@P3: empty,
L324@P3: 3. all successors expect the same parity, and
L325@P3: 4. there exists an inverter that can drive all successors and the
L326@P3: net connecting them.
L327@P3: We interpret each vertex as a 3-dimensional object, where the
L328@P3: area, in which the predecessor can be placed, lies in the x-y-plane,
L329@P3: and the time interval lies on the z-axis.
L330@P3: The new cluster is the 3-dimensional intersection of all successors. If and only if this intersection is nonempty, conditions 1 and
L331@P3: 2 hold.
L332@P3: Now we use a greedy strategy for clustering. At the beginning
L333@P3: the cluster consists only of one successor: the active vertex with
L334@P3: maximum lower bound of its arrival time interval.
L335@P3: In each subsequent step, we look for an active vertex v expecting the same parity, such that the volume of the intersection of the
L336@P3: cluster and v is nonempty and maximum among all choices of v. If
L337@P3: there is no such vertex, we close this cluster. Otherwise we check
L338@P3: if there exists an inverter that can drive the cluster and v. If so, we
L339@P3: add v to the cluster, otherwise we will not look at v in this clustering again. Then we continue with the next active vertex v of the
L340@P3: right parity.

L31@P2: Abstract
L32@P2: We study a special three-sided matching game, the so-called supplier-firm-buyer game, in
L33@P2: which buyers (customers) and sellers (suppliers) trade indirectly through middlemen (firms).
L34@P2: Stuart (Stuart, 1997) showed that all supplier-firm-buyer games have non-empty core. We
L35@P2: show that for these games the core coincides with the classical bargaining set (Davis and
L36@P2: Maschler, 1967), and also with the Mas-Colell bargaining set (Mas-Colell, 1989).

L60@P4: We study a special three-sided matching game, the so-called supplier-firmbuyer game, in which buyers and sellers (suppliers) trade indirectly through middlemen (firms). Stuart (1997) showed that all supplier-firm-buyer games have
L61@P4: non-empty core. We show that for these games the core coincides with the classical bargaining set (Davis and Maschler, 1967), and also with the Mas-Colell
L62@P4: bargaining set (Mas-Colell, 1989).

L66@P4: 1 Introduction
L67@P4: In their seminal paper Shapley and Shubik (1972) introduced assignment games to study
L68@P4: two-sided matching markets where there are indivisible goods which are traded between
L69@P4: sellers and buyers in exchange for money. Their proof of the non-emptiness of the
L70@P4: core established a fruitful research area. Multi-sided assignment games, however, have
L71@P4: different features. Most importantly, the non-emptiness of the core is not guaranteed
L72@P4: anymore even when there are only three sides in the game, as first demonstrated by
L73@P4: Kaneko and Wooders (1982).
L74@P4: Since the core may be empty for multi-sided assignment games, some authors study
L75@P4: conditions to obtain the non-emptiness of the core (see for instance Quint, 1991; Stuart,

L86@P5: In the so-called supplier-firm-buyer games, agents in the market are partitioned into
L87@P5: three sides and the groups are arranged along a chain. Sellers (suppliers) and buyers
L88@P5: (customers) are at the two ends of the chain, but trade between them can only be made
L89@P5: via agents in the middle (firms). The valuation on the supplier-firm-buyer triplets is
L90@P5: locally additive, it sums up the potential values of the supplier-firm and of the firm-buyer
L91@P5: matchings, but it is realized only if all three parties cooperate. Stuart (1997) showed
L92@P5: that all supplier-firm-buyer games have non-empty core.
L93@P5: In order to find plausible payoff allocations even in games with empty core, Aumann
L94@P5: and Maschler (1964) suggested a set-valued solution concept that incorporates some
L95@P5: negotiating possibilities of the players. Among the various bargaining sets proposed,
L96@P5: the one investigated by Davis and Maschler (1967) has emerged, for it was proved to be
L97@P5: non-empty whenever the game has a non-empty imputation set (Davis and Maschler,
L98@P5: 1967). Mas-Colell (1989) introduced another bargaining set notion based on preimputations and showed that it is non-empty for any game. Holzman (2001) proved that
L99@P5: for superadditive games the classical (Davis-Maschler) bargaining set is included in the
L100@P5: Mas-Colell bargaining set.

L62@P1: The parametric shortest path problem is a generalization of the standard singlesource shortest path problem in which some of the edge costs have a parameter
L63@P1: subtracted from them. An instance of the problem is specified by giving a directed
L64@P1: graph G = (V, E, c) with edge costs, a source vertex s with all vertices reachable
L65@P1: from s, and a subset E′ of the edges representing those edges whose costs have
L66@P1: the parameter subtracted from them. Specifically, a particular value λ of the
L67@P1: parameter yields the directed graph Gλ = (V, E, c − λδE′) with edge costs, where
L68@P1: (c−λδE′)(e) = c(e)−λδE′(e), and δE′(e) = 1 if e ∈ E′ and 0 otherwise. (We adopt
L69@P1: the convention that the parameter is subtracted so that influence of parameterized
L70@P1: edges on shortest paths increases with the parameter.)
